Example script takes the elements down from 683 to 330 by including the MeshSizeExtendFromBoundary line

```
import cadquery as cq
small = cq.Workplane().box(1, 1, 1)
big = cq.Workplane(origin=(1,0,0)).box(1,2,2)
assy = cq.Assembly()
assy.add(small)
assy.add(big)
r, o = cq.occ_impl.assembly.imprint(assy)
print(len(r.Faces()))  # prints 12 which is correct
topods = r.wrapped
object_to_pass_to_gmsh=topods._address()

import gmsh
gmsh.initialize()
gmsh.option.setNumber("General.Terminal", 1)
volumes = gmsh.model.occ.importShapesNativePointer(object_to_pass_to_gmsh)
gmsh.model.occ.synchronize()
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.Algorithm", 1)
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeMin", 0.2)
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeMax", 30)
gmsh.option.setNumber("Mesh.MeshSizeExtendFromBoundary", False)
gmsh.model.mesh.generate(2)
gmsh.write("gmsh_of_cadquery_in_memory.msh")
```

The manual meshing with gmsh is mainly to check if the step geometry has errors which mean it can't be meshed. Current Cad-To-Dagmc only offers one mesher whioch is gmsh so if gmesh cna't manually mesh the geometry then Cad-To-Dagmc also can't mesh your geometry.

If you are able to successfully mesh manually in gmsh then you have the option to save the msh file and Cad-To-Dagmc can import the msh file with its MeshToDagmc class https://github.com/fusion-energy/cad_to_dagmc/blob/5cd38e4ddb9c1db86192bace38629a341c41d8cb/src/cad_to_dagmc/core.py#L328C7-L328C18

So, I think I made it work for my case, although I will admit I am making a lot of guesses of what might have been wrong and how the code works.

I disabled all checks regarding the size of the `original_ids`, `scrambled_ids` and `material_tags` / `material_tags_in_brep_order`. The meshing phase (`gmsh, volumes = _mesh_brep(...`) went well, and generated 4266 faces and 770955 nodes (vertices?).
The code went on to the `_vertices_to_h5m` part and spent a lot of time in there, the memory usage increased to 30 GB until the process eventually segfaulted. Looking at the code in the `_vertices_to_h5m` function, it looked like lines 145 and 146 

`moab_verts = moab_core.create_vertices(vertices)`
`moab_core.add_entity(face_set, moab_verts)`

were adding the same vertices repeatedly to the moab_core object (because it is inside two for loops), and so I modified the function for this not to happen, _ie_ I commented out lines 145 and 146 and added `moab_verts = moab_core.create_vertices(vertices)` line 105 right after the moab_core object definition. I did not add back the `moab_core.add_entity(face_set, moab_verts)` line, however.

After this change the _vertices_to_h5m very quickly generated an .h5m file that I mbconverted to a.vtk that looks like my original step file at first glance.

Hello,

Since the last time, I searched the gmsh library for a function to scale the geometry. Unfortunately, I got a bit lost in the documentation and decided to proceed differently.

I found a method that seems to work:

I create my CAD geometry in centimeters, with a scale factor of 1/10. When I import the geometry into gmsh, a factor of 10 seems to be applied to the geometry.

Since these two factors cancel each other out, I then convert the geometry to .h5m format.

I then verify the consistency of the distances with openmc_plot, and with this method, it seems that I achieve the desired importation with the correct dimensions. I'm able to conduct simulations that more closely resemble what I should expect.

Typically the generation of mesh files involves the definition of vertices once and the triangle elements define their connectivity based on those existing vertices. Alternatively, as triangles are added one can check for an existing vertex, but this can be computationally expensive in its own right.

FWIW, MOAB comes with an `mbmerge` tool that will handle the removal of redundant vertices. This may help with file sizes, but it won't solve the generation time issue of course.

Just a few options that allow us to change the dagmc model after creation when using it in openmc.

## option 1

The common material tags for difference cells can also be changed on openmc side

```python
Model.differentiate_mats()
```

https://docs.openmc.org/en/stable/pythonapi/generated/openmc.model.Model.html#openmc.model.Model.differentiate_mats 

This will assign new materials for each material that appears in more than one cell

## option 2

make use of CellFilters instead of MaterialFilters. CellFilters can accept a cell ID and we can get the cell ID using ```dagmc_h5m_file_inspector```

```python
import dagmc_h5m_file_inspector as di

di.get_volumes_and_materials("dagmc.h5m")

>>> {1: 'small_box', 2: 'big_box'}
```

https://github.com/fusion-energy/dagmc_h5m_file_inspector#finding-volume-ids-with-their-materials

using openmc lib

https://docs.openmc.org/en/stable/pythonapi/generated/openmc.lib.dagmc_universe_cell_ids.html#openmc.lib.dagmc_universe_cell_ids

```

### What this PR gives us and what's left to wire it up

`write_vtk()` is the right building block for letting the **`cad-to-dagmc-mesher`** backend emit an unstructured `.vtk` volume mesh without gmsh. Today only the gmsh backend can write `.vtk` (via `gmsh.write()`), even though the mesher already produces tetrahedra — they're just discarded. To finish the job:

**1. Stop discarding the tets from the mesher**

`mesh_assembly()` already returns a `"tet_data"` key whenever a solid has `target_edge_length` set:

```python
result["tet_data"] = { solid_id: {
    "vertices":    [[x, y, z], ...],      # local, per-solid indexing
    "tetrahedra":  [[v0, v1, v2, v3], ...],
    "boundary_vertices": ..., "boundary_triangles": ...,
    "recovery_stats": {...},
}}
```

But `_mesh_with_cad_to_dagmc_mesher()` in `core.py` only returns `vertices, triangles_by_solid_by_face, material_tags` — it drops `tet_data`. It needs to also return (or separately expose) `tet_data`.

**2. Combine the per-solid tet meshes into one mesh**

Each solid's `tetrahedra` indices are **local to that solid's `vertices` list**. To produce a single unstructured grid you must concatenate the vertex arrays and offset each solid's tet indices by the running vertex count before handing them to `write_vtk()`.

**3. Wire `write_vtk()` into the export paths**

- `export_dagmc_h5m_file()`: the unstructured branch is currently gated on `if meshing_backend == "gmsh" and unstructured_volumes:` — add the mesher case that calls `write_vtk()`.
- `export_unstructured_mesh_file()`: currently gmsh-only (`init_gmsh` → `gmsh.write`). Add mesher-backend support here too.

**4. Match the gmsh/MOAB output format (agreed direction)**

The goal is output equivalent to what gmsh writes today. The MOAB-written reference (`tests/single_volume_thin.vtk`) includes `POINT_DATA`/`CELL_DATA` `SCALARS GLOBAL_ID int` blocks that this PR's writer omits:

```
POINT_DATA 25530
SCALARS GLOBAL_ID int 1
LOOKUP_TABLE default
...
CELL_DATA 39432
SCALARS GLOBAL_ID int 1
LOOKUP_TABLE default
```

Open question that must be answered before we can call the minimal writer "sufficient": does `openmc.UnstructuredMesh(..., library="moab")` **require** GLOBAL_ID, or does it just read it opportunistically? If required, `write_vtk()` needs to emit those blocks. Also worth confirming whether `VTK DataFile Version 2.0` vs `3.0` matters to the MOAB reader.

**5. Add a round-trip transport test**

The current tests only assert the ASCII text is well-formed. We need a test that meshes a solid with the mesher backend, writes the `.vtk`, loads it via `openmc.UnstructuredMesh(filename, library="moab")`, and runs a small transport/tally — this is what actually proves the file is usable and settles the GLOBAL_ID question.

**6. Related cleanup**

`vtk` is currently listed under the `tests` extra in `pyproject.toml` (and installed in the conda CI workflows) but is **not imported anywhere** — all `.vtk` writing goes through gmsh. It can be removed independently of this PR. Once the mesher backend writes its own VTK, there's no remaining reason to reintroduce a `vtk` runtime dependency.

## Verified fix

Giving faces that compare equal the same id is enough. Faces are compared with `TopoDS_Shape.IsSame`, which is what CadQuery's `Shape.__eq__` and `Shape.__hash__` already use, and the imprint guarantees the shared face is the same underlying face in both solids, so a dict keyed on the face works directly.

Against `cadquery_direct_mesh_plugin/plugin.py`:

```diff
     # Solid and face IDs need to be unique unless they are a shared face
     solid_idx = 1  # We start at 1 to mimic gmsh
     face_idx = 1  # We start at id of 1 to mimic gmsh
+    # Imprinting makes the face shared between two solids the same underlying
+    # face, so faces that compare equal (TopoDS_Shape.IsSame) must be given the
+    # same id. Otherwise each solid contributes its own copy of the interface
+    # and the h5m ends up with two coincident surfaces instead of one shared
+    # surface, leaving the model non watertight at that interface.
+    face_ids_by_face = {}

@@
-            face_triangles[face_idx] = cur_triangles
+            if face in face_ids_by_face:
+                this_face_idx = face_ids_by_face[face]
+            else:
+                this_face_idx = face_idx
+                face_ids_by_face[face] = this_face_idx
+
+            face_triangles[this_face_idx] = cur_triangles

             # Move to the next face
-            face_idx += 1
+            if this_face_idx == face_idx:
+                face_idx += 1
```

Results on the two touching cuboids from the report, with the geometry check and the transport comparison from the same run:

| | surfaces | shared interfaces | material 1 | material 2 |
|---|---|---|---|---|

## Unrelated observation

While tracking this down, note that `cad_to_dagmc.core` is not reachable as a module attribute:

```python
>>> import cad_to_dagmc.core as core
>>> core.__file__
'.../pymoab/core.cpython-313-x86_64-linux-gnu.so'
```

`core.py` does `from pymoab import core, types` and `__init__.py` does `from .core import *`, so the re-exported `core` name overwrites the `cad_to_dagmc.core` submodule attribute with pymoab's `core`. It does not affect normal use of the public API, but it makes `cad_to_dagmc.core` misleading to import and could bite anyone reaching for internals. Happy to raise it separately if useful.

Fix submitted upstream as jmwright/cadquery-direct-mesh-plugin#10, with a regression test that fails without the change. Once released, cad_to_dagmc should pick it up through a version bump of `cadquery_direct_mesh_plugin`.

Correction on the unrelated `cad_to_dagmc.core` observation above: that is already fixed on main. The pymoab import was moved inside `define_moab_core_and_tags` in a try/except for the `PyMoabNotFoundError` message, so there is no longer a module level `core` binding to be re-exported by `from .core import *`:

```python
>>> import sys; sys.path.insert(0, "src")
>>> import cad_to_dagmc.core as core
>>> core.__file__
'.../src/cad_to_dagmc/core.py'
```

Looking at how the stop decision is made, the ideal mesh never needed more memory than the machine had. **The forecast that stopped refinement was more than 2x too high.** This points to a fix that keeps the full refinement and makes the result independent of RAM.

## The forecast, not the RAM

Before each round, `mesh_assembly` forecasts its peak as `previous_peak * growth` (`_REFINE_MEMORY_GROWTH = 3.0` until two rounds have been measured). `previous_peak` comes from `_peak_rss_bytes()`, the process's lifetime `ru_maxrss`.

- **The lifetime high-water mark includes the imprint.** That's often the most memory-hungry step, and it's cached after round 0, so later rounds don't repeat it. Here it was about 4.1 GB after round 0.
- **The 3x factor was measured with every solid's tolerance halved.** Here round 1 refined 50 of 64 solids, mostly small winding packs, so far less meshing work than that.
- **Forecast 4.1 x 3 = 12.4 GB**, just over the 12.3 GB budget, so refinement stopped.
- **The same refinement on the idle machine ran to completion, and the whole job peaked at 5.1 GB** (`/usr/bin/time -v`), imprint included. The real cost was well under half the forecast.

## Trade time for memory instead of quality

The resulting mesh should depend only on the inputs. A tighter memory limit should make meshing slower, not produce a different mesh. Thread count is a weak lever for refinement: it drives imprint memory (8.59 against 1.09 GB on 22 against 1 thread, per the `imprint_threads` docstring), but the imprint is cached after round 0. What drives a refinement round's memory is how much is meshed and held at once. So:

1. **Re-mesh only the solids that need it.** Each round currently re-meshes the whole assembly, although only the folding solids and their neighbours change. Keep the other solids' triangles from the previous round.
2. **Mesh in bounded batches** (one solid, or a few at a time), so a round's peak is set by the largest batch, not the whole model. If a batch would exceed the budget, shrink the batch, and drop threads where that helps, rather than stopping refinement.
3. **Forecast from the work actually scheduled.** For example, the triangles in the solids being refined, times the expected growth for their new tolerance, measured per round rather than from the lifetime high-water mark.
4. **Treat the user's thread and memory settings as upper limits.** The mesher can go below them to fit, and it should always reach the same final mesh. A smaller or busier machine just takes longer.

With those changes, the "stop early and keep a worse mesh" branch would only be needed when a single solid on its own can't fit in memory. That case should be a loud error rather than a different h5m.

Closing in favour of keeping "all" as the default. The memory growth per imprint thread that motivated this is model dependent: on a 72-solid model of medium B-spline sectors that touch on spline faces, imprint went from 540 s on 1 thread to 322 s on 2 with peak memory flat at 2.5 GB, so a fixed cap of 4 would waste cores there. `imprint_threads` remains the setting to lower on memory-limited machines with large spline models.
